subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the:
options: Total value of goods and services produced within a country in a period
questions.explain: GDP is a key measure of a nation's economic output/activity.

questions.q: The four components of aggregate demand are consumption, investment, government spending and:
questions.explain: AD = C + I + G + (X - M).

questions.q: A fall in the general price level, ceteris paribus, causes a:
options: Movement along AD (higher real output demanded)
questions.explain: A price-level change causes a movement along AD; other factors shift the curve.

questions.q: In the short run, an increase in aggregate demand tends to raise:
options: Both real output and the price level
questions.explain: Higher AD raises output (and employment) and, especially near capacity, the price level.

questions.q: The long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve in the monetarist/new classical view is:
options: Vertical at the full-employment level of output
questions.explain: LRAS is vertical at potential output, determined by the quantity and quality of factors of production.

questions.q: The business cycle describes fluctuations in:
options: Real GDP over time (booms and recessions)
questions.explain: Phases include expansion, peak, contraction/recession and trough.

questions.q: A recession is commonly defined as:
options: Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP
A single month of rising prices
questions.explain: A recession is a period of declining real output.

questions.q: Cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment is caused by:
options: A lack of aggregate demand during a downturn
questions.explain: Falling AD in a recession reduces the demand for labour, causing cyclical unemployment.

questions.q: Structural unemployment arises from:
options: A mismatch between workers' skills/location and available jobs
questions.explain: Structural unemployment reflects changes in the economy's structure (e.g. declining industries).

questions.q: Demand-pull inflation is caused by:
options: Excess aggregate demand pulling up the price level
questions.explain: When AD outpaces AS near full capacity, the price level is bid up.

questions.q: Cost-push inflation is caused by:
options: Rising costs of production (e.g. wages, raw materials)
questions.explain: Higher costs shift SRAS left, raising prices and reducing output (possible stagflation).

questions.q: Inflation is usually measured using a:
questions.explain: The CPI tracks the price of a representative basket of goods and services over time.

questions.q: Sustained high inflation harms an economy by:
options: Eroding the real value of money and savings
questions.explain: Inflation reduces purchasing power and can create uncertainty that discourages investment.

questions.q: Contractionary monetary policy to reduce inflation typically involves:
questions.explain: Higher interest rates reduce borrowing and spending, lowering AD and inflationary pressure.

questions.q: Monetary policy in most economies is conducted by the:
questions.explain: The central bank sets interest rates and influences the money supply.

questions.q: Expansionary fiscal policy involves:
options: Increasing government spending and/or cutting taxes
questions.explain: Fiscal policy uses the government budget to influence AD; expansionary policy boosts AD.

questions.q: To close a recessionary (deflationary) gap, a government could use:
questions.explain: Boosting AD helps move the economy back towards full employment.

questions.q: Supply-side policies aim to:
options: Increase the productive capacity (LRAS) of the economy
questions.explain: Measures such as training, infrastructure and deregulation raise potential output.

questions.q: The Lorenz curve is used to illustrate:
questions.explain: The further the Lorenz curve bows from the line of equality, the greater the inequality.

questions.q: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 to 1, where a higher value indicates:
questions.explain: A Gini of 0 means perfect equality and 1 means maximum inequality.

questions.q: Frictional unemployment refers to people who are:
questions.explain: Frictional unemployment is short-term as workers search for or move between jobs.

questions.q: An increase in business confidence would most likely:
options: Shift aggregate demand to the right (more investment)
questions.explain: Greater confidence raises investment (and consumption), increasing AD.

questions.q: Progressive taxation helps reduce income inequality because:
options: Higher earners pay a larger proportion of their income in tax
questions.explain: Progressive taxes take a rising share of income as income rises, redistributing resources.

questions.q: Economic growth is best defined as an increase in:
options: Real GDP (or real GDP per capita) over time
questions.explain: Real (inflation-adjusted) output growth measures a genuine rise in production.
